title: Birding in Neora Valley: seasons, sites and costs
meta_description: Plan birding in Neora Valley National Park from Lava, Lolegaon and Kolakham: best months, forest zones, target species, permits, guides and honest costs.
summary: Neora Valley National Park spans about 183 m to 3,200 m, so a few days around Lava, Kolakham and Lolegaon cover tropical, temperate and high forest birds. Go from November to April, start at dawn, hire a local guide, and enter the park on a day permit from Lava. It is closed mid-June to mid-September.

sections.heading: Why Neora Valley is special for birds
paras: Neora Valley National Park was set up in 1986 and covers about 88 sq km of Kalimpong district. Its lowest edge, near Samsing in the Dooars, sits around 183 m; its top, Rachela Danda on the Sikkim and Bhutan side, reaches about 3,200 m. Few places in India pack that much height into so small an area, and every few hundred metres of climb brings a different forest and a different set of birds.

Much of the park is steep and roadless, which has kept the forest intact. Visitors see only the edges: the jeep track from Lava to Zero Point, the forest-edge villages of Kolakham and Rishyap, the heritage forest at Lolegaon and the lower forests reached from Samsing and Mouchuki. That is still enough to fill a notebook. Mammals share the same forest, among them red panda, Himalayan black bear, goral, serow, barking deer and clouded leopard, though most are rarely seen.

paras: The simplest way to plan is by height. Each zone below is reachable on a day from Lava or the Dooars. Species listed are ones local guides regularly find; nothing is guaranteed.

sections.heading: When to go
paras: November to April is the season. In winter, November to February, many birds of the high forest move down the slopes to escape the cold, a pattern called altitudinal migration. Mixed flocks of laughingthrushes, sibias, minlas, yuhinas and tits then feed along the Lava, Rishyap and Kolakham roads at dawn, and you can see thirty species in an hour without walking far. Mornings at Lava are near freezing, so dress for it.

March and April are the second peak. Birds sing, breeding plumage shows, and rhododendron, magnolia and orchids flower in the upper forest, which brings sunbirds and other nectar feeders. Haze and afternoon showers increase, and leeches appear on wet paths. May is warmer and wetter with fewer flocks.

The park is closed from about 16 June to 15 September for the monsoon. Late September and October are green and quiet, but the forest is wet and many birds are hard to find in dense foliage. Check current status before you travel, as opening dates move after heavy rain.

sections.heading: The main birding sites
paras: Most visiting birders base themselves at Lava for two nights, then add one night each at Kolakham and Lolegaon. These are the places we send people, in rough order of priority.
list: Lava to Zero Point: a jeep track of about 13 km inside the park, through oak, fir, rhododendron and bamboo. Drive slowly at dawn, stop for every flock, then walk from Zero Point with the forest guide.
Lava–Rishyap road: about 11 km climbing to around 2,590 m through rhododendron and oak, good for mixed flocks and pheasants at first light.
Lava town edge: the forest lanes above the WBFDC lodge and around the monastery, worth an hour at dusk.
Kolakham and the Changey Falls trail: about 900 m each way, with forktails and wagtails by water and woodpeckers and barbets in the trees.
Lolegaon heritage forest: old cypress and pine with canopy walkways about 180 m long, useful for treecreepers, nuthatches and canopy feeders at eye level.
Samsing and Mouchuki: the lower, warmer face of the park from the Dooars, with a different set of species; pair it with Gorumara.

sections.heading: Permits, guides and costs
paras: Indian and foreign visitors enter Neora Valley on a day permit issued by the forest range office in Lava. Entry costs about ₹120–150 per Indian and ₹500 per foreigner, a vehicle fee about ₹300–500, a permitted jeep to Zero Point and back ₹1,500–2,500, and a compulsory forest guide ₹300–600 per group, indicative 2026. A camera fee may also apply. Carry photo ID. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

A forest guide is required, but he is not necessarily a bird specialist. For serious birding, hire a local bird guide as well, about ₹1,500–3,000 a day, indicative 2026. Several young guides from Lava and Lolegaon know calls, flock routes and the spots where pheasants feed at dawn, and they work well with the forest staff. Book them through your lodge or a planner before you arrive, especially for November and March weekends.

Keep costs down by sharing the park jeep: it takes up to six and costs the same for two. Stay at the forest corporation's lodges in Lava and Lolegaon, which put you on the forest edge so you can bird on foot before breakfast without a car.

sections.heading: Red panda and other hopes
paras: Many visitors come hoping for a red panda. Neora Valley is one of the few protected habitats of the species in West Bengal, along with Singalila in Darjeeling district, and the animals live in the upper forests with dense bamboo. They are shy, spend much of the day high in trees, and are most active at dawn and dusk. Very few visitors see one. Treat a sighting as luck, and go for the forest and the birds. If you want a sure view, the Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park in Darjeeling runs a red panda breeding programme.
The same applies to satyr tragopan, a spectacular red pheasant of the high forest. It is present but seldom seen by day visitors. A calling bird in spring is a fine reward in itself.

sections.heading: Good field habits
paras: Birding here is quiet, slow work, and the forest is shared with villagers and other visitors. A few habits help everyone.
list: Start at first light; activity drops sharply after about 10 am.
Wear earth-coloured clothes and keep voices low, especially in jeeps.
Do not use call playback inside the park; it stresses breeding birds and is discouraged by forest staff.
Stay on permitted tracks and follow your forest guide's instructions.
Carry binoculars of your own; spares are rare locally.
Pack leech socks from March to May and in late September.
Take all litter out, including fruit peels and tissues.

faqs.q: What is the best month for birding in Neora Valley
faqs.a: November to April, with two peaks. December to February brings altitudinal migrants down into easy reach along the Lava roads, with cold mornings. March and April bring song, breeding plumage and flowering rhododendrons. The park is closed from about 16 June to 15 September; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many bird species are found in Neora Valley
faqs.a: Neora Valley holds a long list of species thanks to its range of altitudes, from about 183 m to 3,200 m, and lists published by birders run to several hundred species. A four-day visit around Lava, Kolakham and Lolegaon with a good guide in winter or spring commonly produces a list of well over a hundred, depending on weather and effort.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for birding in Neora Valley
faqs.a: Yes, to enter the national park. Day permits are issued at the forest range office in Lava, with entry about ₹120–150 per Indian and ₹500 per foreigner, plus vehicle and guide fees, indicative 2026. Roads and villages outside the park, such as the Rishyap road, Kolakham and Lolegaon, need no permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see a red panda in Neora Valley
faqs.a: It is possible but rare. Red pandas live in the park's higher bamboo and fir forest, mostly up in trees, and are active at dawn and dusk. Very few visitors see one. Your best chance is a quiet dawn walk with a forest guide beyond Zero Point between November and April. The Darjeeling zoo offers a sure view.

faqs.q: Where should birders stay for Neora Valley
faqs.a: Lava is the main base, two nights, because the park permit office and jeeps are there; the WBFDC Lava Eco Tourism Centre sits on the forest edge. Add a night at Kolakham for the Changey Falls trail and a night at Lolegaon for its heritage forest. For the lower forest, stay at Samsing or Mouchuki on the Dooars side.

faqs.q: How much does a bird guide cost in Neora Valley
faqs.a: About ₹1,500–3,000 a day for an experienced local bird guide, indicative 2026, in addition to the compulsory forest guide inside the park, ₹300–600 per group. Rates depend on the guide's experience and season. Book ahead for November, December and March weekends, when good guides are busy.

faqs.q: Is Neora Valley good for bird photography
faqs.a: Yes, though light is often low in the forest and birds move fast in mixed flocks. Roadsides at Lava, Rishyap and Kolakham give better light than deep forest trails. A camera fee may apply inside the park. Drones are not allowed. Patience at flowering or fruiting trees in spring often gives the best results.

faqs.q: Can beginners enjoy birding in Neora Valley
faqs.a: Yes. Mixed flocks along the roads are easy to watch, and a local guide will name birds and calls for you. Bring binoculars and a field guide or app, and do not worry about lists. Non-birding companions usually enjoy the forest, Kanchenjunga views and village homestays.

faqs.q: What else lives in Neora Valley apart from birds
faqs.a: The park protects red panda, Himalayan black bear, goral, serow, barking deer, wild boar and clouded leopard, along with many butterflies, orchids and rhododendrons. Most mammals are shy and rarely seen by day visitors. Barking deer and squirrels are the most common sightings from the Zero Point track.
